sentences.text: The name Cimoliopterus combines the Greek words for chalk and wing.
The first specimen was found in the Grey Chalk Subgroup of Kent, England, and described as Pterodactylus cuvieri in 1851.
In 2013, Brazilian paleontologists Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner reviewed species previously assigned to the genus Ornithocheirus.
The genus Cimoliopterus was described by Rodrigues and Kellner in 2013.
Cimoliopterus likely fed by dipping its long jaws into water to catch fish with interlocking teeth.
In 2006, André J. Veldmeijer and colleagues noted that the interlocking teeth of ornithocheirids were built for spearing slippery prey like fish rather than cutting.

Researchers suggested that because their teeth were not adapted for chewing, these pterosaurs might have pre-digested small fish before swallowing, a process requiring cheeks or throat pouches reported in some pterosaurs.
Cimoliopterus was likely adapted for long-distance oceanic soaring, supported by fossils found mainly in marine settings.
Like pterosaurs in general, ornithocheirids probably took flight by launching quadrupedally and were possibly able to swim well enough to take off from water surfaces.
Ornithocheirids' terrestrial locomotion was likely limited by short legs, restricting them to slow shuffling walks or faster bounding, indicating they spent limited time on the ground.
It is debated whether the premaxillary crests were used to stabilize jaws during feeding or served as display structures.
Witton considered pterosaur crests to be display structures rather than stabilizers, as they are thought to be sexually dimorphic in some species.
Rodrigues and Kellner suggested in 2013 that the crest of Cimoliopterus evolved independently from that of anhanguerids due to its different position.
Pêgas and colleagues agreed in 2019 that the Cimoliopterus crest evolved independently because its closer relatives lacked crests.
A sculpture of the pterosaur is shown in a quadrupedal pose with one foot flat on the ground.
In 2019, Cimoliopterus was classified in the family Cimoliopteridae within the clade Targaryendraconia, with Camposipterus as its closest relative.
Peter Wellnhofer stated in 1991 that the genus Ornithocheirus was a wastebin of species from different countries needing clearer definition.
In 1870, Seeley classified the species under the name Ornithocheirus cuvieri within a group he named Ornithocheirae.
Researchers found the jaw expansion in Aetodactylus and Cimoliopterus unclear as a precursor to the rosette-like jaws of anhanguerians.
Cimoliopterus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in areas that are now England and the United States.
The discovery of Cimoliopterus dunni in North America showed that European and North American pterosaur faunas were similar in the mid-Cretaceous despite the widening Atlantic Ocean.
Cimoliopterus is a pteranodontoid closely related to Aetodactylus, which is also found in Cenomanian strata in Texas.

The holotype of C. cuvieri was found in Kent, England, in chalks and marls of the Grey Chalk Subgroup dating to the Cenomanian-Turonian ages of the Upper Cretaceous, though its precise stratigraphic position is unknown.
While Seeley speculated the depression above the first tooth pair in C. colorhinus was for lip attachment, Rodrigues and Kellner questioned this in 2013, noting pterosaurs likely had horny beaks.
It is uncertain whether C. colorhinus had a crest because all known specimens are incomplete.
It remains debated why no close ties exist between North and South American pterosaurs, suggesting a possible dispersal barrier.
